chapterTitle: The LMAX Disruptor and Lock-Free Ring Buffers

beats.headline: Why do standard queues choke at high throughput?
beats.subline: It isn't just code—it's hardware contention killing your performance.
beats.narration: ArrayBlockingQueue is reliable, but it hits a wall at millions of messages per second. If you want microsecond-level latency, you need to understand why standard queues fail.

beats.title: Locking vs. Lock-Free

bottom.label: Disruptor

beats.narration: Blocking queues use ReentrantLocks, which park threads and trigger expensive kernel context switches. The Disruptor uses sequence numbers and memory barriers to coordinate without ever blocking.

beats.title: The False Sharing Problem
beats.subtitle: Why adjacent fields destroy performance

nodes.label: Cache Line (64 bytes)
nodes.detail: Head, Tail, and Count fields sit here

beats.narration: False sharing happens when head and tail indices sit on the same cache line. Updating one invalidates the other across cores, forcing constant, silent hardware synchronization.

beats.title: The Power-of-Two Trick

steps.explanation: Integer division is a multi-cycle instruction.
Bitwise AND is one cycle. Requires power-of-two size.

beats.narration: Modulo arithmetic is slow. By enforcing a power-of-two buffer size, we replace division with a bitwise AND, turning a multi-cycle instruction into a single-cycle operation.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Single vs Multi-Producer Sequencers →
beats.narration: That's the foundation. In Part 2, we compare the Single-Producer and Multi-Producer sequencers to see how we avoid CAS loops entirely.

beats.headline: Do you really need a CAS loop?
beats.subline: Most developers over-engineer their concurrency. Here is how to avoid atomic overhead.
beats.narration: Atomic Compare-And-Swap is expensive. If you have a single producer, you don't need it. Let's look at how the Disruptor optimizes for your specific topology.

beats.title: Producer Types
beats.narration: Single-producer mode is lightning fast because it avoids CAS entirely. Multi-producer mode uses CAS to claim slots, but introduces a hazard: consumers might see a claimed slot before the data is written.

beats.title: The Available Buffer
beats.subtitle: Preventing garbage reads in multi-producer
beats.narration: To prevent reading partial data, we use an availableBuffer. Each slot tracks a 'lap' flag. Consumers scan this buffer and stop at the first slot that hasn't been published yet.

beats.title: Single-Producer Logic

steps.explanation: Only check gating sequences when necessary.

beats.narration: The single-producer sequencer is brilliant. It only checks the slowest consumer's position when the buffer is actually full. Most of the time, the producer just increments its counter.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): Wait Strategies & CPU Pinning →
beats.narration: That's the sequencer architecture. In Part 3, we explore Wait Strategies—the difference between 100% CPU usage and microsecond latency.

beats.headline: Busy spinning vs. yielding: which is faster?
beats.subline: Your choice of wait strategy determines if your app is a racecar or a battery hog.
beats.narration: When a consumer catches up to the producer, it must wait. Do you spin, yield, or sleep? The wrong choice can destroy your latency or starve your OS.

beats.title: Wait Strategy Trade-offs
beats.narration: BusySpin is the fastest but pegs your CPU at 100%. Only use it if you have isolated cores. If you're on a shared container, YieldingWaitStrategy is the safer bet.

beats.title: The Spin-Wait Hint

steps.explanation: Crucial for ARM/x86 performance. Throttles the loop and frees resources.

beats.narration: Always use Thread dot onSpinWait inside your loops. It emits the PAUSE instruction, which throttles the spin, reduces heat, and lets hyper-threaded siblings actually do work.

beats.title: Wait Strategy Hierarchy
beats.subtitle: Latency vs. CPU Utilization
beats.narration: Choose your strategy based on your environment. HFT engines use BusySpin on pinned cores. General enterprise apps should stick to Blocking or Sleeping strategies to save power.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Match strategy to your CPU budget
beats.narration: That's the wait strategy trade-off. In Part 4, we wrap up with the diamond topology and show you how to wire it all together in production.

beats.headline: How to wire complex pipelines without copying data?
beats.subline: The Disruptor's diamond topology allows parallel processing on the same event.
beats.narration: Need to journal an order and replicate it simultaneously? Don't copy the object. Use the diamond topology to share the same ring buffer across multiple handlers.

beats.title: Diamond Pipeline
beats.subtitle: Parallel fan-out, serialized fan-in
beats.narration: The diamond topology lets you run parallel tasks like journaling and replication. The final stage only runs once both parallel tasks are complete, ensuring total consistency.

beats.title: Wiring the Pipeline

steps.explanation: Journal and Replicate run at the same time.
MatchingEngine waits for both to finish.
Always publish in finally to avoid hangs.

beats.narration: Wiring is simple. Use handleEventsWith for parallel tasks and dot then for sequential dependencies. And always publish in a finally block—if you miss this, your consumers will hang forever.

beats.title: Final Checklist
beats.caption: Production best practices
beats.narration: Pre-allocate your objects to avoid GC churn. Use power-of-two sizes. And if you're serious, pin your threads. Check out the branch below for the full implementation.

takeaways: Use diamond topology for parallel tasks
